title: Trends Across a Period and Down a Group
keyIdea: Across a period, protons are added but the inner shells stay the same, so the pull on the outer shell rises: atoms get smaller and their outer electrons get harder to remove. Down a group, each atom has an extra shell, so the outer electrons are further out and more shielded: atoms get bigger and the outer electrons are easier to remove. Metals react by losing electrons, so they get more reactive down a group; non-metals react by gaining them, so they get less reactive.

kid: An atom is a tug of war. The protons in the nucleus pull on the outer electrons. The inner electrons sit in the way and block some of that pull. We call this shielding.

Go across period 3, from sodium to chlorine. Each step adds one proton and one outer electron. The inner shells stay the same, 2 and 8. So the pull on the outer shell grows, and the atom shrinks from 0.186 nm to 0.099 nm.
Go down Group 1, from lithium to caesium. Each atom has one more shell. The outer electron is further out, with more shielding in the way. It is easier to pull off, so the metals get more reactive.

The energy to remove the first outer electron is the first ionisation energy. It rises across a period and falls down a group. Two small dips across period 3, at aluminium and sulfur, come from sub-shells.
adult: A useful model is the core charge: the nuclear charge minus the inner electrons. Across period 3 it rises from about +1 at sodium to +7 at chlorine. Electrons in the same shell shield each other only a little, so the outer shell is pulled closer and the radius falls. The data are 0.186 nm for Na and 0.099 nm for Cl; argon has no comparable bonded radius.

First ionisation energy follows the same pull. It rises from 496 kJ/mol for Na to 1521 kJ/mol for Ar. Down Group 1 it falls from 520 kJ/mol for Li to 376 kJ/mol for Cs. The core charge stays near +1, but the outer electron is further out and better shielded, so it is held less tightly.

The dips are real. Al is lower than Mg because its outer electron is in 3p, which is higher in energy than 3s and partly shielded by it. S is lower than P because one 3p orbital now holds a pair, and the paired electrons repel.

Common mistakes: saying chlorine is bigger because it has more electrons; thinking more protons down a group means a tighter hold, when distance and shielding win; using a new shell to explain the Al and S dips, when all period 3 atoms use shell 3; and giving non-metals the metal trend. Halogens react by gaining an electron, so their reactivity falls down the group.

familyTip: With a periodic table, take turns pointing at two elements in the same period or the same group. The other person says which atom is bigger and which loses an electron more easily, and gives the reason using protons, shells and shielding.

practice.prompt: Why is a chlorine atom smaller than a sodium atom?
choices: Chlorine has more protons pulling on the same shells
Chlorine has more electrons, which pack tighter
practice.hint: Both atoms have three shells. What changes from Na to Cl?
practice.explain: From Na to Cl the nuclear charge rises from 11 to 17 while the inner shells stay 2, 8, so the outer shell is pulled in.

practice.prompt: A period 3 atom has {p} protons and 10 inner electrons. What is its core charge? (Give the number only.)
practice.hint: Core charge is the nuclear charge minus the inner electrons.
practice.explain: Core charge = {p} − 10 = {=p-10}, so the outer electrons feel a pull of about +{=p-10}.

practice.prompt: Which has the larger atoms: the Group 1 metal in period {a} or the one in period {b}?
practice.hint: Each period down adds a shell.
practice.explain: Period {b} is lower, so its atom has more shells and a larger radius than the atom in period {a}.

practice.prompt: Why does potassium react faster with water than sodium?
choices: Its outer electron is further out and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
It has more protons, so it holds electrons tighter
It has a larger core charge
practice.hint: Metals react by losing their outer electron. Which atom loses it more easily?
practice.explain: Both have core charge +1, but potassium's outer electron is in shell 4, further out and more shielded, so its first ionisation energy is lower (419 vs 496 kJ/mol).

pool.prompt: How does atomic radius change across a period from left to right?
pool.hint: Think of the core charge with the same inner shells.
pool.explain: The rising nuclear charge pulls the same outer shell closer, so radius decreases across a period.

pool.prompt: First ionisation energy falls down Group 1 even though the number of protons rises. Why?
choices: The outer electron is further away and more shielded
pool.hint: What changes as each new shell is added?
pool.explain: The extra shells put the outer electron further out behind more inner electrons, which outweighs the rising nuclear charge.

pool.prompt: Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?
choices: Al's outer electron is in 3p, higher in energy and shielded by 3s
Al's outer electron is in a new shell
pool.hint: Write the outer sub-shells: Mg 3s², Al 3s² 3p¹.
pool.explain: The 3p electron starts slightly higher in energy and is partly shielded by the 3s pair, so it takes less energy to remove.

pool.prompt: Why is the first ionisation energy of sulfur lower than that of phosphorus?
choices: Two 3p electrons share an orbital and repel
Sulfur has an extra inner shell
pool.hint: Draw the 3p boxes for P (3p³) and S (3p⁴).
pool.explain: In sulfur one 3p orbital holds a pair, and the repulsion between them makes one easier to remove.

pool.prompt: The first ionisation energy of sodium is 496 kJ/mol. How many kJ are needed to remove one electron from each atom in {n} mol of sodium atoms?
pool.hint: First ionisation energy is given per mole of atoms.

pool.prompt: Which reacts more vigorously: chlorine or bromine?
pool.hint: Halogens react by gaining an electron. Which atom pulls an incoming electron harder?
pool.explain: Chlorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it attracts an extra electron more strongly and is more reactive.

pool.prompt: Element A has core charge +{a} and element B has core charge +{b}; both are in period 3. Which atom is smaller?
pool.hint: Same inner shells, so the bigger core charge pulls harder.
pool.explain: With the same inner shells, core charge +{b} pulls the outer shell in more than +{a}, so that atom is smaller.

pool.prompt: Across period 3, what happens to the shielding of the outer electrons?
choices: It increases a lot with each element
pool.hint: How many inner electrons does every period 3 atom have?
pool.explain: Every period 3 atom has the same 10 inner electrons (2, 8), so shielding stays roughly constant while nuclear charge rises.

pool.prompt: Which of these has the highest first ionisation energy?
pool.hint: Look at the right-hand end of the period.
pool.explain: Argon has the highest core charge in period 3 and the smallest outer shell, so its first ionisation energy is 1521 kJ/mol.

visual.caption: Does this make the outer electrons easier or harder to remove? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: shrink period 3 atoms, pull off outer electrons, explain the dips and judge which atom reacts more.
